prompt: In a Dockerfile, why does `COPY package*.json ./` followed by `RUN npm ci` come before `COPY . .`?
choices: So that the dependency-install layer stays cached across rebuilds when only application source code changes, not dependencies
Because Docker requires package.json to be copied before any other file
It has no effect on caching; the order is purely stylistic
So that npm ci can see the compiled output from the build step

prompt: What does `EXPOSE 3000` actually do in a Dockerfile?
choices: Publishes port 3000 so it's reachable from outside the container
Documents which port the container listens on; it does not publish or forward that port by itself
Opens a firewall rule on the host machine
Sets the port the application's process binds to at runtime

prompt: In a multi-stage build, what happens to the builder stage's filesystem (its full node_modules, compilers, devDependencies) once the build finishes?
choices: It is merged into the final image as a compressed layer
It is kept in a separate registry for debugging
It is discarded entirely unless explicitly copied out with COPY --from=builder
It is kept only if the Dockerfile doesn't specify a runtime stage

prompt: An app container in a docker-compose.yml needs to reach a database service named `db` on the same compose file. What hostname should its connection string use?
choices: localhost
db
the host machine's LAN IP address

prompt: You run `docker compose down` (without -v) on a stack that has a named volume for Postgres data. What happens to that data?
choices: It is deleted along with the containers
It is preserved, because named volumes outlive the containers unless -v is passed
It is automatically backed up to the host's home directory
It depends on whether the containers were started with --build

prompt: Why does omitting a .dockerignore file pose the same kind of risk as committing generated/local state to git?
choices: It doesn't -- .dockerignore is purely a build-speed optimization with no correctness implications
Without it, COPY . . can bake local secrets (like a .env file) and machine-specific artifacts permanently into image layers, just as committing state breaks a repo's reproducibility
It only affects which files are visible inside docker exec sessions
It determines which files get pushed to a registry after the image is already built

prompt: A single-stage Dockerfile using `FROM node:20` produces a 1.24GB image. Switching to a multi-stage build with a `node:20-slim` runtime stage drops it to 231MB. What accounts for most of that size difference?
choices: The slim image uses a more efficient compression algorithm for the same files
The build-time-only tooling and devDependencies (compilers, TypeScript, @types packages) are no longer present in the final image
Slim images don't include the application's own compiled code
node:20-slim runs a different, faster version of Node.js

prompt: What is the practical effect of `depends_on` between two services in a docker-compose.yml, by default?
choices: It controls container start order only; it does not wait for the depended-on service to be ready to accept connections
It guarantees the dependent service won't start until the other service passes a health check
It automatically retries the dependent service's connection until the other service is reachable
It creates a dedicated private network between just those two services
